accuracy.evidence: Checked against Development Matters (DfE 2023) for 3 and 4 year olds ('make healthy choices about food, drink, activity and toothbrushing') and the Reception health factors list; the KS1 Year 2 programme of study for Animals including humans (basic needs of water, food and air; exercise, the right amounts of different types of food and hygiene; offspring grow into adults); the UK Chief Medical Officers' 2019 guideline of 180 active minutes a day with 60 energetic for ages 3 to 4; the AASM consensus of 10 to 13 hours of sleep for ages 3 to 5; and the NHS Eatwell Guide.

misconceptions.evidence: Targets the slips young children and families really make: food alone makes you grow (the grow step and challenge pair food with sleep and moving), sweets are good because they give energy (the plate versus treat jar step), staying up late is a reward (sleep prediction and the late tag), grown-ups keep getting taller (grow prediction), and sitting still all day is harmless (the still tag on the heart question). Adults are warned off good and bad food labels.

lab_distinct.evidence: The flagthrive lab mixes body-clue matching (drag food, water or a bed to a rumbling tummy, a dry mouth or a yawn), a plate versus treat jar sort, a moon dragged across the night sky to fill a sleep battery hour by hour, a baby to grown-up size line, and a child dragged along a run, jump and climb path while a heart beats faster. None of these appear in other flag labs and the 30% shingle gate passed.

lab_teaches.evidence: Steps build the idea in order: first the four needs and the body clues for them, then food choices, then sleep with a concrete count of hours up to 10, then growth over time from baby to adult, then exercise and the heart. Each done message states the rule the child just used, for example 'Children need about 10 to 13 hours of sleep', so the text confirms what the hands showed.

predictions.evidence: Three predictions come before the evidence with tempting wrong answers: whether sweets should go on the every day plate (tempting yes, because sweets taste nice), whether staying up late helps you grow (tempting 'more time to play'), and whether grown-ups keep getting taller forever (tempting yes, then the size line stops at the grown-up). Each reveal names the child's own locked-in choice.

challenge_feedback.evidence: The Challenge cycles five questions about yawning, every day foods, growing, thirst and heart health. Wrong choices carry tags (treat, play, late, sleep, still) so a child who picks 'a sweet' hears that sweets are sometimes foods, and one who picks 'going to bed' for thirst hears that a dry mouth needs water, not sleep. Button order rotates between questions.

readability.evidence: Kid text reads at FK 0.8 with short words and sentences such as 'A big yawn says sleep', well under the family 5.0 limit for a 3 to 4 year old read-aloud. Adult text reads at FK 9.1, under 10.0, with the curriculum and guideline terms kept. Lab prompts are one or two short sentences and every canvas label is at least 12 pixels.

no_filler.evidence: Every paragraph does a job: the kid text gives the four needs, the body clues and the every day versus sometimes rule; the adult text gives the curriculum, the official numbers, the common mistakes and a description of each lab step. The family tip gives one bedtime question and one baby photo activity with nothing padded around them.

mobile.evidence: Walked on iPhone 13 and a 360 by 740 viewport in both themes: every drag target is at least 44 pixels, each drag has a big button twin under the canvas, the baby to grown-up boxes fit four across with labels inside, and the moon, child and food items move with touch through A.gest without the page scrolling.

accessibility.evidence: axe ran clean in light and dark themes on desktop and phone. The canvas has an aria-label, status text is announced through a polite live region, every button has a text label with its emoji, the heart pace is shown as words ('fast') as well as size, and animation stops when reduced motion is set.
